---
title: "Lab · Pico Identity Declaration"
---

In this lab you will author full identity declarations for two Picos that
will later form a relationship, and validate them with the `pico` CLI.

## Setup

Create a scratch working directory and export the `pico` CLI per the
[Hello Pico one-time setup](../../../../labs/hello-pico/objectives.html#one-time-setup):

```bash
mkdir -p scratch/identity
```

## Step 1 — Author Pico A's identity

Create `scratch/identity/pico-a.yaml`:

```yaml
# scratch/identity/pico-a.yaml
id: oep.pico.alice
identity:
  type: did
  public:
    method: webvh
    url: https://engine-a.example.com/picos/alice/did.json
relationships:
  - did:peer:rel-alice-bob
```

## Step 2 — Author Pico B's identity

Create `scratch/identity/pico-b.yaml`:

```yaml
# scratch/identity/pico-b.yaml
id: oep.pico.bob
identity:
  type: did
  public:
    method: webvh
    url: https://engine-b.example.com/picos/bob/did.json
relationships:
  - did:peer:rel-bob-alice
```

## Step 3 — Validate both declarations

```bash
pico parse scratch/identity/pico-a.yaml --out /tmp/pico-a.json \
  && echo "OK: Pico A parses"
pico parse scratch/identity/pico-b.yaml --out /tmp/pico-b.json \
  && echo "OK: Pico B parses"
```

## Step 4 — Extend Pico A with a second relationship

Add a second relationship to `pico-a.yaml` representing a new relationship
with Pico C, then re-run the parse:

```bash
pico parse scratch/identity/pico-a.yaml --out /tmp/pico-a.json \
  && echo "OK: Pico A with two relationships parses"
```

## What you will produce

Two valid YAML identity declarations plus a demonstration that a Pico can
carry multiple `did:peer` relationships under a single `did:webvh`.
